job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our Social Science class today, we simulated how a state government is formed. We learned that a state is divided into specific areas called constituencies, which are based on population rather than existing district boundaries. During the election, voters in each constituency choose one representative, known as a Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA). Once the results are in, the party that secures more than half of the total constituencies wins the majority. This winning party then selects their leader, who is appointed as the Chief Minister by the Governor. It is important to note that the Chief Minister is not directly elected by the public; instead, they are chosen by the MLAs of the party that holds the majority in the assembly. Our activity showed that a party needs a clear majority of seats to form the government, not just having the highest number of votes compared to other individual parties. This process ensures that the government represents the will of the majority of the elected representatives, who are the direct voice of the people in their respective areas.

items.evidence: We learned that a state is divided into specific areas called constituencies, which are based on population rather than existing district boundaries.
items.q: A state has 30 districts. Why might it not have exactly 30 constituencies?
options: Constituencies are drawn by population, not district lines
Each district must send exactly two MLAs
Constituencies are fixed by the Governor's office
Big districts are joined into one constituency
items.explain: Constituencies are based on population, not on district boundaries, so their number need not match the districts.

wrong.why: thinks a constituency is the same as a district
gives the Governor a role the passage never mentions
invents a rule from district size

items.evidence: It is important to note that the Chief Minister is not directly elected by the public; instead, they are chosen by the MLAs of the party that holds the majority in the assembly.
items.q: How does a person become the Chief Minister of a state?
options: Winning party's MLAs choose a leader for the post
Voters across the state pick one person by ballot
The Governor picks any MLA from any party
The MLA with the most votes is chosen
items.explain: The majority party's MLAs choose their leader, and the Governor appoints that leader; the public does not elect the Chief Minister.

wrong.why: thinks the people elect the Chief Minister directly
thinks the Governor chooses freely, ignoring the majority party
thinks the biggest vote-winner automatically becomes Chief Minister

items.evidence: Our activity showed that a party needs a clear majority of seats to form the government, not just having the highest number of votes compared to other individual parties.
items.q: In a 100-seat assembly, Party X wins 35 seats and every other party wins fewer. What follows?
options: Party X cannot form the government on its own
Party X forms the government as the largest party
Party X forms it after the Governor's approval
Party X forms it if its leader wins big
items.explain: A party needs more than half the seats, so 35 of 100 is not enough to form the government.

wrong.why: thinks the party with most seats forms the government
thinks the Governor's approval can replace a majority
thinks winning the most votes is enough

items.evidence: This process ensures that the government represents the will of the majority of the elected representatives, who are the direct voice of the people in their respective areas.
items.q: Why is a government backed by the majority of MLAs seen as fair?
options: MLAs are the people's direct voice, so it reflects their will
MLAs work only for the party that is in power
Voters can order each MLA to follow their wishes
MLAs from every party share the Chief Minister's post
items.explain: MLAs are the direct voice of the people, so a majority of them reflects the people's will.

wrong.why: thinks MLAs work only for the ruling party
thinks MLAs must do whatever voters ask
thinks power is shared among all parties
